analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to get your permission before tracking and sharing your phone's location, with new anti-stalking penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill, with six Democratic senators behind it, got one subcommittee hearing in June 2014 and never received a vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal rule that companies cannot collect or share the location data from your phone or other devices without your clear, explicit permission. It created exceptions for emergencies, parents tracking children, and court orders or law enforcement. It also criminalized selling or building 'stalking apps' that track someone without their knowledge, created an Anti-Stalking Fund from seized stalking devices to pay for law-enforcement training and victim hotlines, and let individuals sue companies that violate the consent rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who carries a phone or drives a connected car. The bill required companies to tell you what location data they collect, who they share it with, and let you withdraw consent at any time, and it gave you the right to sue. It also directly protected victims of domestic violence and stalking, whose abusers use hidden tracking apps to follow them.

how_it_helps.text: Companies could not knowingly collect or share device location data without the user's affirmative, express consent after clear notice naming who the data may be shared with.
Large collectors of location data would have to run a public website disclosing what they collect, why, whom they share it with, and how to revoke consent.

The bill made it a federal crime to disclose location data to aid interstate stalking or domestic violence, and banned the manufacture, distribution, and advertising of location-tracking 'stalking apps,' with the seized devices and proceeds funding law-enforcement training and stalking hotlines.
Individuals could sue violators for damages up to $5,000 per violation per day, plus attorney's fees, and the Attorney General could also bring civil actions.

Federal surveys would begin tracking how location technology is used to facilitate domestic violence, sexual assault, and stalking, and the Justice Department would run a complaint center and grant program on geolocation stalking crimes.

analysis.who_pays: Companies whose business models rely on collecting and reselling location data without explicit permission — app developers, mobile advertising networks, and data brokers — would have to obtain consent, publish what they do with the data, and face civil penalties and, for some, criminal liability. Consumers would see more consent prompts and notices.
analysis.who_pays_short: App developers and mobile ad companies

drawbacks.text: Total civil penalties against a company were capped at $1,000,000 for related violations unless the conduct was willful or intentional, which critics could say lets large companies treat violations as a cost of business.
The bill allowed law enforcement to obtain location data without the user's consent under any lawful authority, preserving a significant government access channel.
Compliance would impose real costs on small app developers, and the bill's core rules would not take effect until 180 days after the Attorney General issued regulations, delaying any protection.
The bill would supersede weaker state rules while allowing stronger state consumer-protection laws to stand, creating a two-tiered legal landscape companies would have to navigate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the benefits are substantial and concrete: control over one of the most sensitive kinds of personal data, and targeted protection for stalking and domestic-violence victims. The costs are mostly compliance burdens and consent friction for companies, and the bill's own penalty cap limits how aggressively violators could be pursued. The main weakness is not what the bill did but what it left out — it exempts telecommunications carriers' activities already regulated under the Communications Act, so the largest holders of location data faced no new consent requirement from this bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee after introduction, got a single subcommittee hearing, and was never voted on by the full committee or either chamber before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Al Franken introduced the bill on March 27, 2014, joined by Sens. Coons and Warren as original cosponsors; five Democratic senators cosponsored in total.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, where it sat with no further action.
On June 4, 2014, the Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology and the Law held a hearing on the bill, but the full committee never took it up.
No roll-call vote on the bill ever occurred in either chamber of the 113th Congress, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting and selling smartphone location data kept operating under the old rules, with no federal consent requirement, no public disclosure of what they collect, and no private right of action for consumers. People being tracked by hidden apps through phones had no new federal recourse.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee

against.name: Mobile app and advertising industries
against.role: Companies and trade groups whose revenue depends on location-based advertising and data sharing
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed mandatory consent requirements for location tracking during debates over this and earlier versions of the legislation.

sides.party_line_note: All six senators attached to the bill were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it; because no vote ever occurred, the partisan split was never tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Mobile app developers and location-based advertising companies
industries.note: Their core data-collection practice — gathering precise location and sharing it with third parties without explicit permission — would become unlawful without consent, with public disclosure requirements and civil penalties. Consumers would gain control over data these companies currently monetize invisibly.

The bill exempted activities already regulated under sections 222 and 631 of the Communications Act, so carriers faced no new federal consent rule from this bill. They keep their existing legal regime governing customer location data.

The bill criminalized manufacturing, distributing, possessing, and advertising devices that intercept location data, with forfeiture of the devices and proceeds. These products exist primarily to track victims of stalking and abuse.
An Anti-Stalking Fund, Justice Department training grants, a public complaint center, and new survey data on technology-facilitated abuse would fund and inform their work protecting victims.
